## Abstract {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Tagma[^tagma] is a 16-bit coordinate primitive: a fixed Unicode block (U+AC00--U+D7A3) with a closed-form composition formula, three independent axes, and zero collision probability. The primitive is substrate-independent. Its definition is one formula, and its realizations differ only in the material that evaluates it. The software realization is the reference implementation in Rust and C++ [^syntagma] [^refimpl]; the hardware realization is the subject of this whitepaper series: a combinational decoder with its inverse (the compose unit) and the field-wise distance unit, a gate-level synthesis flow, FPGA demos on the Upduino 3.1 (iCE40UP5K) and the iCESugar-Pro (ECP5), and a chton SRAM segment store modeled behaviorally pending the macro.

Everything in this series is measured, not claimed. The decoder is verified exhaustively over all 11,172 valid code points in three independent channels (formula, Rust reference, gate netlist), and formal equivalence proves the RTL and the synthesized netlist identical over all 2^16 inputs. The measured gate count is 478 cells in the ev-compatible generic schema and 588 cells in a 2-input gate-level estimate, with 201 LUT4 plus 41 carry cells on iCE40. The demo closes the 12 MHz board clock at 16.79 MHz Fmax (59.55 ns critical path after place and route). A two-stage pipelined decoder emits one code point per clock and closes register to register at 77.69 MHz on the ECP5, and a self-checking build runs that pipeline against the combinational reference at 40 MHz on the board.

Two findings frame the series. First, the ~300 gate claim of the Tagma whitepaper holds for the naive shift-subtract decoder (206 to 232 cells), but timing closure on a 12 MHz board requires a multiply-shift structure that costs roughly 2.5x more gates. Second, the hardware is not a speedup for the N=1 dense case: the entire 11,172-entry space fits in L1 cache, which the software already exploits at 0.38 ns per access. The hardware value is energy, determinism, and physical embedding, not per-operation speed. The streaming track does not change that ranking. A pipelined decoder at 77.69 MHz emits 77.69 million code points per second, while the L1 path at 0.38 ns per access implies about 2.6 billion accesses per second, so what pipelining adds is continuous flow and a fixed cost per code point rather than a faster dense decode.

## Scope and relation to the primitive

The hardware track does not redefine Tagma. The composition formula, the axis ranges, and the 11,172-entry space are identical to the software definition:

$$C(i,m,f) = \text{U+AC00} + 588i + 28m + f, \quad 0 \leq i < 19,\; 0 \leq m < 21,\; 0 \leq f < 28$$

What changes is the substrate. The software realization evaluates the formula with arithmetic in Rust; the hardware realization evaluates it with logic gates. The two must agree on every input, and the verification pipeline in this series enforces exactly that. The layer map is shown in Figure @fig-hw-layers.

:::{ layout-ncol=1 }

{{< include ../_include/bench/fig-hw-layers.qmd >}}

:::

One boundary correction is part of this work: the last valid code point is U+D7A3, not U+D7AF. The block contains exactly 11,172 code points and U+AC00 + 11,171 = U+D7A3. Inputs in U+D7A4..U+D7AF decode to an out-of-range initial axis and are structurally invalid; the `tagma_core` reference documents these as filler positions.

## Realization status

The claim of this series is bounded by what is realized. The three operations of the primitive are realized as RTL and verified end to end: the decoder, the compose unit (the decoder's inverse), and the distance unit. The gate-level netlist simulation and the formal-equivalence check cover all three.

A separate realization is on a device rather than in gates: the record layer addressed by coordinates, over a flash partition on an ESP32-S3, with no operating system under the engine. It exercises the software stack and the medium, not the RTL decoder, and it is reported as the [minimum-class device run](/projects/syntagma/tagma/#sec-minimum-device).

One item is documented but not yet realized: the segment store is a behavioral model of the address map, pending the OpenRAM macro that needs a PDK install. The physical demonstration runs on the iCESugar-Pro: the demo builds, the bitstream is written to configuration flash and boots, and the validity output drives the onboard RGB LED. The external switch and LED wiring that turns it into a decoder demonstration is the remaining step. The streaming design is realized further, because it needs no external wiring: its source is an internal counter, and the build compares the pipeline against the combinational reference on the device. Where a result depends on an unrealized item, the document states the dependency in place.

## Hardware reference

The realization lives under `hw/` in the syntagma repository. The toolchain is open source end to end: Verilator for simulation, Yosys for synthesis, nextpnr-ice40 and icepack for the iCE40 target, icetime for its timing analysis, nextpnr-ecp5 and ecppack for the ECP5 target, and OpenRAM for the memory macro. Two boards are supported, each with its own constraint format and clock: the Upduino 3.1 (iCE40UP5K-SG48, PCF, 12 MHz) and the iCESugar-Pro (ECP5 LFE5U-25F-6BG256C, LPF, 25 MHz).

| Artifact | Purpose | Location |
|----------|---------|----------|
| `tagma_decoder` | 3-axis combinational decoder | `hw/rtl/tagma_decoder.v` |
| `tagma_decoder_tb` | exhaustive testbench, formula and golden modes | `hw/rtl/tagma_decoder_tb.v` |
| `tagma_compose` | axis-to-index compose, the decoder inverse | `hw/rtl/tagma_compose.v` |
| `tagma_dist` | field-wise distance of two code points | `hw/rtl/tagma_dist.v` |
| `tagma_segment_store` | segment store behavioral model, 11,172 x 16-bit | `hw/rtl/tagma_segment_store.v` |
| `tagma_demo_top` | board demo, registered outputs | `hw/rtl/tagma_demo_top.v` |
| `tagma_decoder_pipe` | two-stage streaming decoder, one code point per clock | `hw/rtl/tagma_decoder_pipe.v` |
| `tagma_pipe_top` | counter-sourced streaming top, register-to-register timing | `hw/rtl/tagma_pipe_top.v` |
| `tagma_pipe_check_top` | on-device comparison of the pipeline against the reference | `hw/rtl/tagma_pipe_check_top.v` |
| `golden_anchors.hex` | 11,172 vectors from the Rust reference | generated by `make golden-export` |
| `check_golden_anchors.py` | consistency gate over the anchor file | `hw/tools/` |
| synthesis flows | generic, gate-level, iCE40 | `hw/synth/yosys/synth_*.ys` |
| PnR flow | bitstream and timing report | `hw/synth/yosys/run_pnr.sh` |
| `chton_sram.py` | OpenRAM configuration | `hw/openram/` |

The reference definition is the Rust `tagma_core`.

## Measured results summary

The numbers below are the authoritative hardware figures for the Tagma primitive. They replace the approximate "300 gates in 28nm" phrasing in earlier software documents with measured values from the open toolchain (Yosys, nextpnr, icetime). The gate trade-off is shown in Figure @fig-hw-gates and the clock closure in Figure @fig-hw-fmax.

| Metric | shift-subtract (naive) | multiply-shift (current) |
|--------|------------------------|--------------------------|
| Generic cells (ev schema) | 206 | 478 |
| Gate-level estimate (2-input) | 232 | 588 |
| iCE40 LUT4 + SB_CARRY | 95 + 66 | 201 + 41 |
| PnR ICESTORM_LC (UP5K) | 177 | 255 |
| Logic levels | 72 | 33 |
| Critical path | 115.90 ns | 59.55 ns |
| Fmax | 8.63 MHz | 16.79 MHz |
| Meets 12 MHz board clock | no | yes |

The same RTL on the ECP5 device measures 50 TRELLIS_COMB and 16 TRELLIS_FF out of 24,288, 33 I/O, and 4 multipliers, with a 22.85 ns worst reported path against a 25 MHz clock. That figure is the worst cross-domain path, input to register; the design has no register-to-register path for nextpnr to constrain, so no Fmax is reported. The 59.55 ns figure above is the whole critical path icetime reports for the placed iCE40 design. The two are device results, not a speedup, and the comparison is stated that way in the FPGA document.

Pipelining changes what the tool can report at all. The streaming top takes its code from a counter, so its paths run register to register, and nextpnr-ecp5 reports a clock for the first time. The self-checking build adds the combinational reference to the same die, which is why its ceiling is lower: the reference is three multipliers deep, and it is the slower of the two.

| Metric | Pipeline alone | Self-check build |
|--------|----------------|------------------|
| Clock | 25 MHz board oscillator | 40 MHz from the 25 MHz oscillator |
| Fmax, register to register | 77.69 MHz | 55.86 MHz |
| Fmax, reference path | not present | 50.00 MHz |
| TRELLIS_COMB | 39 | 165 |
| TRELLIS_FF | 43 | 120 |
| MULT18X18D | 4 | 7 |
| Latency | 2 clocks | 2 clocks |
| Throughput | 1 code point per clock | 1 code point per clock |

The self-check clock is 40 MHz rather than the 50 MHz the PLL also produces, because the reference path measures 19.48 ns, which leaves 2.6 percent of margin at 50 and 28 percent at 40.

## Verification pipeline

Every hardware artifact is checked against the Rust reference, which is the single source of truth for the primitive's behavior. The golden exporter writes the full coordinate decomposition to a vector file; the RTL simulation and the gate-level simulation both read it; the formal equivalence check closes the loop between the RTL and the synthesized netlist. The pipeline is shown in Figure @fig-hw-verify.

:::{ layout-ncol=1 }

{{< include ../_include/bench/fig-hw-verify.qmd >}}

:::

The channels and the commands that produce them:

| Channel | Command | Coverage |
|---------|---------|----------|
| Formula simulation | `make sim` | all 11,172 code points |
| Golden anchors | `make sim-golden` | all 11,172, against the Rust reference |
| Gate-level netlist | `make gatesim` | all 11,172, against the same anchors |
| Formal equivalence | `make equiv` | all 2^16 inputs, RTL against netlist |
| Compose | `make sim-compose`, `make sim-compose-golden`, `make gatesim-compose` | all 32^3 axis combinations, 11,172 anchors |
| Distance | `make sim-dist`, `make sim-dist-golden`, `make gatesim-dist` | 11,172 code points against two references and a varying-operand sweep |
| Streaming | `make sim-pipe` | 4 full sweeps, 44,689 emitted triples against the combinational decoder |
| Compose and distance equivalence | `make equiv` | 2^15 axis combinations, 2^32 input pairs |

`hw/tools/check_golden_anchors.py` gates the regenerated anchor file against the decomposition contract, so a stale or corrupted export fails before any simulation starts.

The pipeline runs in CI through `make -C hw check` in the syntagma repository, so the numbers in this series are reproducible from a clean checkout when Verilator and Yosys are installed.

## Engineering decisions

| Decision | Rationale | Consequence |
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| Multiply-shift over shift-subtract | 72 to 33 logic levels, closes the 12 MHz board clock | 206 to 478 generic cells |
| Golden anchors from Rust, regenerated | single source of truth, no drift | the anchor file is a build artifact, regenerated in CI |
| Four verification channels | formula, reference, netlist, equivalence | RTL and netlist proven identical over 2^16 inputs |
| Registered demo outputs | one-cycle latency measurable with a real clock | Fmax and setup checkable with icetime |
| LED polarity as a parameter | the Upduino's onboard LED is negative logic, the iCESugar-Pro's RGB LED is active high | `led_valid` is driven from `LED_ACTIVE_LOW`, default 1 for the Upduino, 0 on the Pro |
| Explicit width-matched Verilog | Verilator `-Wall` clean without hiding truncation | concat-based zero-extension, lint only for unused bits |
| Two-stage pipeline split at the multiplier boundary | each stage carries one multiplier, which is what makes one code point per clock reachable | 77.69 MHz register to register on the ECP5, latency of two clocks |
| Self-check compiled into the board build | a place-and-route result is not an observation of the board | the pipeline and the reference are compared every clock on the device, and a mismatch latches an indication |
| ev-compatible `stat -json` flow | numbers comparable across the SSCCS stack | emittable as neXus Facts later |

## Development notes

- The boundary correction is a documentation item as well as a testbench item: every document that states the range as ending at U+D7AF should be checked, and `tagma_core` records U+D7A4..U+D7AF as filler positions.
- Toolchain notes: Verilator requires explicit width-matched operands and lint scoping for intentional truncation; icetime needs the iCE40 chipdb discoverable (a Homebrew symlink on macOS); the anchor file is a language-neutral contract that can gate a C++ port later.

| Track | Step | Dependency |

| Physical demo | wire the switch and LED modules per the board constraints and capture the demo; the iCESugar-Pro bitstream is programmed and boots | switch and LED modules |
| Standard cell | the OpenROAD Sky130 flow runs end to end and is re-run in the syntagma hw CI job; two flow bugs are recorded in the devlog | none |
| chton propagation | generate the segment store SRAM from `chton_sram.py` and attach it to the decoder | OpenRAM and PDK |
| Power model | run the OpenROAD power analysis on the VCD trace from `make sim-trace` | standard cell flow |
| Multi-target | one RTL builds for iCE40 (`BOARD=upduino31`) and ECP5 (`BOARD=icesugar_pro`); Artix-7 remains open | ECP5 done, Artix-7 needs a board |
| Streaming | the two-stage pipeline emits one code point per clock and closes at 77.69 MHz; the self-checking build compares it against the reference at 40 MHz on the device | none; the three indicator observations close it |
